:question/problem "Let $V=C[0,2\pi ]$ be the vector space of all functions that are continuous on $[0,2\pi ],$ equipped with the inner product 

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(t)g(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Given the functions $f(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡t$ and $g(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t),$ which of the following statements are true?

I. $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=2\pi $

II. $⟨f(t),g(t)⟩=0$

III. $f(t)⊥g(t)$ with respect to the inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ in $V$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the identity $\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )).$*" :question/worked-solution "We need to evaluate

$$
⟨f(t),g(t)⟩={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

We can evaluate this integral using the given identity, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(t-2t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(t+2t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(-t)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)}{3}){|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\pi )-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi )}{3}]-\frac{1}{2}[\operatorname{cos}⁡0-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡0}{3}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now examine the statements:

- Statement I is false, while statement II is true. This is as a result of the above calculations.

- Statement III is true. Since the inner product is zero, our vectors must be orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d2a7c0e4-497b-555e-b210-485ed2c4815e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d2a7c0e4-497b-555e-b210-485ed2c4815e" :answer-field/id #uuid "d2a7c0e4-497b-555e-b210-485ed2c4815e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4dd94adf-0738-5e8a-8201-c8eaf6da5741" :answer-field/choices ["answer-688f977f-48f9-5555-8bb1-1d938d96b3a5" "answer-bd83ca4f-fc8b-5c42-9c89-2ce30742bfbd" "answer-4dd94adf-0738-5e8a-8201-c8eaf6da5741" "answer-354f5fb0-502e-5b97-96b1-1770af96065f" "answer-390a92f2-20da-56ad-8a6d-81f1d663abf6"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-688f977f-48f9-5555-8bb1-1d938d96b3a5" :answer/id #uuid "688f977f-48f9-5555-8bb1-1d938d96b3a5" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bd83ca4f-fc8b-5c42-9c89-2ce30742bfbd" :answer/id #uuid "bd83ca4f-fc8b-5c42-9c89-2ce30742bfbd" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4dd94adf-0738-5e8a-8201-c8eaf6da5741" :answer/id #uuid "4dd94adf-0738-5e8a-8201-c8eaf6da5741" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-354f5fb0-502e-5b97-96b1-1770af96065f" :answer/id #uuid "354f5fb0-502e-5b97-96b1-1770af96065f" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-390a92f2-20da-56ad-8a6d-81f1d663abf6" :answer/id #uuid "390a92f2-20da-56ad-8a6d-81f1d663abf6" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135101 :tutorial/content "Let $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ be vectors in a vector space $V$ equipped with an inner product $\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle.$ 

Two vectors $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ are **orthogonal with respect to the inner product** $\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle$ in $V$ if their inner product is zero:

$$
\langle \mathbf{x} , \mathbf{y} \rangle = 0
$$

If the two vectors are orthogonal, then we denote this by $\mathbf{x} \perp \mathbf{y}.$ For instance, the vectors 

![](images/3d/3d118ca8f8b3ea3e1b978d7bcd0159b1774ea4e8848f39d3a2566e6931b4c2f2.svg)

in $\mathbb{R}^3$ equipped with the inner product

$$
\langle \mathbf{x} , \mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1y_1 + 2x_2y_2 + x_3y_3
$$

are orthogonal, since

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨x,y⟩ & =1\cdot 2+2\cdot (1\cdot (-1))+0\cdot 3 \\  & =2-2+0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** The zero vector $\mathbf{0}$ in a vector space $V$ equipped with an inner product $\langle \cdot , \cdot \rangle$ is orthogonal to any vector $\mathbf{x} \in V$ since $\langle \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{x} \rangle = 0.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133987 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204105 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3689d124-7069-5ac1-b495-7dcfa807134a" "question-5bab4cd0-ae02-5029-8d61-df09bcee19e2" "question-17f34adc-72ed-5271-a021-3a7f1d773e6b" "question-6b5fc782-a821-5ef2-823c-11a0d288b2b3" "question-2633d33a-0706-5b9b-a985-6a0050cda4a1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203875 :question/problem "Suppose we have a dataset consisting of $4$ datapoints with $2$ features in the form of the $4 \times 2$ matrix
![](images/23/232f6bffd41437d85b7a0f09ec268d459009656ef77fba4b4fb445b52dd13a1d.svg)
where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is $0$ and the standard deviation is $1$).
We are also given the SVD decomposition $X = U \Sigma V^T$ where:

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =[\begin{aligned}-0.689 & -0.424 & 0.495 & 0.318 \\ 0.143 & -0.241 & -0.524 & 0.804 \\ 0.695 & -0.188 & 0.650 & 0.244 \\ -0.149 & 0.853 & 0.241 & 0.439\end{aligned}] \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}2.075 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.294 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}-0.709 & -0.706 \\ 0.706 & -0.709\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Find the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance." :question/worked-solution "The one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance is the projection onto the first principal component.

Recall that the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix $X^TX.$ Using the SVD $X = U\Sigma V^T$ and the orthogonality of $U,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}^{T}X & =(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}{U}^{T}UΣ{V}^{T} \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}Σ{V}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\Sigma^T\Sigma$ is diagonal with the squared singular values on the diagonal, the eigenvectors of $X^TX$ are the columns of $V,$ and the eigenvalues are the squared singular values. The largest eigenvalue corresponds to the first singular value $\sigma_1 = 2.075,$ so the first principal component is $v_1,$ the first column of $V{:}$

![](images/e9/e91c75818de82c4564584df51a72432ebc97c90dd5a1c8687b24bd31998d9910.svg)

To obtain the one-dimensional version of the data, we project $X$ onto $v_1$ by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}X{v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}1.40 & -0.62 \\ 0.01 & 0.43 \\ -0.85 & 1.19 \\ -0.56 & -1.00\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-0.709 \\ 0.706\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1.43 \\ 0.30 \\ 1.44 \\ -0.31\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equivalently, we can compute this projection using $u_1 \sigma_1,$ where $u_1$ is the first column of $U.$ Indeed, from the SVD,

$$
\begin{aligned}X{v}_{1} & =UΣ{V}^{T}{v}_{1}=UΣ[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=U[\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]={u}_{1}{\sigma }_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $u_1$ and $\sigma_1 = 2.075,$ we get

![](images/14/148bc9bd4289245d9ada00da68f7b6e0666bfa9c3fffd47fde79164b177732d8.svg)

which confirms the result.

**Watch out!** The vector $v_1$ itself is the first principal component *direction* — a unit vector in feature space. It is not a one-dimensional representation of the data. The one-dimensional representation is $Xv_1$ (or equivalently $u_1\sigma_1$), which is a $4 \times 1$ vector containing the projection of each data point onto this direction." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204106 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-9ccff77b-7d01-5bd7-aaf4-9fba844066ae" "question-3158298f-c612-536d-8b25-00f57fa2f77e" "question-439142f8-6932-5f54-8d84-ca7931d891df" "question-c6804c35-f8e1-5715-b170-24ee05ad3186"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186203876 :question/problem "Suppose we have a dataset consisting of $5$ datapoints with $3$ features in the form of the $5 \times 3$ matrix

If we wish to preserve $75\%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to 
![](images/ab/abbb30d852a431e139075cbe6686ea1aafd697e5d52351e1f23730545ea2d661.svg)." :question/worked-solution "In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible. 

We should pick components based on $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{the amount of cumulative variance preserved}}.$

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are

$$
\sigma_1 = 2.272, \qquad
\sigma_2 = 2.031, \qquad
\sigma_3 = 1.659.
$$

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\dfrac{\sigma_1^2}{\sum\limits_{i=1}^3 \sigma_i^2} =
\dfrac{2.272^2}{2.272^2 + 2.031^2 + 1.659^2} \approx 42.9\%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\dfrac{\sum\limits_{i=1}^2 \sigma_i^2}{\sum\limits_{i=1}^3 \sigma_i^2} =

$$

Thus, we obtain that

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $42.9\%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $77.1\%$ of the variance.

Let's walk through the process of reducing the dimensionality of the dataset." :question/worked-solution "We will use principal component analysis to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset. The first principal component is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{the direction in feature space}}$ with the $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{most}}$ variance.

The second principal component is the direction $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{orthogonal}}$ to the first $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{principal component}}$ with the most variance.

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\text{standardize the data}}.$

The standardized data matrix is

![](images/15/159be3f32150b2a56f4a335990cef0c71cf6362447fc4aff521751743ab2ef58.svg)

The SVD of the standardized data matrix is

$$

:question/problem "Suppose we have a dataset consisting of $4$ datapoints with $2$ features in the form of the $4\times 2$ matrix

$$
X=[\begin{aligned}-0.27 & 0.39 \\ -0.99 & -1.23 \\ -0.13 & -0.28 \\ 1.39 & 1.12\end{aligned}]
$$

where the data has been standardized (the mean of each feature is $0$ and the standard deviation is $1$).
We are also given the SVD decomposition $X=UΣ{V}^{T}$ where:

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =[\begin{aligned}0.035 & 0.86 & 0.132 & 0.491 \\ -0.657 & -0.314 & -0.208 & 0.653 \\ -0.121 & -0.196 & 0.969 & 0.092 \\ 0.743 & -0.351 & -0.032 & 0.569\end{aligned}] \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}2.389 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.542 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}0.707 & -0.707 \\ 0.707 & 0.707\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following matrices corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance?

I. $[\begin{aligned}0.035 \\ -0.657 \\ -0.121 \\ 0.743\end{aligned}]\cdot 2.389$

II. $[\begin{aligned}0.707 \\ 0.707\end{aligned}]$

III. $[\begin{aligned}0.035 \\ 0.86 \\ 0.132 \\ 0.491\end{aligned}]\cdot 2.389$" :question/worked-solution "The one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance is the projection onto the first principal component.

Recall that the principal components are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix ${X}^{T}X.$

Using the SVD and the fact that $U$ is orthogonal (i.e., ${U}^{T}U=I$), we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}^{T}X & =(UΣ{V}^{T})^{T}(UΣ{V}^{T}) \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}{U}^{T}UΣ{V}^{T} \\  & =V{Σ}^{T}Σ{V}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $Σ$ is a diagonal matrix, and so is ${Σ}^{T}Σ,$ we know that the eigenvectors of ${X}^{T}X$ are the columns of $V.$

In particular, the first principal component is the eigenvector of ${X}^{T}X$ corresponding to the largest eigenvalue. 
And since $Σ$ contains the corresponding singular values (square roots of the eigenvalues) in decreasing order, the first principal component is ${v}_{1},$ the first column of $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

- Option I corresponds to the one-dimensional version of the data that preserves the most variance. Notice that it represents ${u}_{1}\cdot {\sigma }_{1},$ where ${u}_{1}$ is the first column of $U$ and ${\sigma }_{1}$ is the first singular value. But this equals  $X\cdot {v}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}X\cdot {v}_{1} & =UΣ{V}^{T}\cdot {v}_{1}=UΣ\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=U\cdot [\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{1} \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]={u}_{1}\cdot {\sigma }_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

- Option II represents ${v}_{1},$ which is the first principal component. It represents a direction in feature space, not a version of the data. Notice that it is also dimensionally incorrect, since it is a $2\times 1$ matrix instead of $4\times 1.$

- Option III uses the values of the first row of $U$ multiplied by ${\sigma }_{1}.$ However, the projection corresponds to the first column of $U.$ Thus, using the row vector is incorrect.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-87da0997-109c-5d59-8556-8db99822494e"] :db/ensure {{field-2}}." :question/worked-solution "In reducing the dimensionality of the dataset, we aim to preserve as much of the original variance as possible. 

We should pick components based on $\text{the amount of cumulative variance preserved}.$

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=2.878,\,{\sigma }_{2}=2.152,\,{\sigma }_{3}=1.636,\,{\sigma }_{4}=0.652.
$$

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{2.878}^{2}}{{2.878}^{2}+{2.152}^{2}+{1.636}^{2}+{0.652}^{2}}≈51.7%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{2.878}^{2}+{2.152}^{2}}{{2.878}^{2}+{2.152}^{2}+{1.636}^{2}+{0.652}^{2}}≈80.6%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first three principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{2.878}^{2}+{2.152}^{2}+{1.636}^{2}}{{2.878}^{2}+{2.152}^{2}+{1.636}^{2}+{0.652}^{2}}≈97.3%.
$$

Thus, we obtain that

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $51.7%$ of the variance,

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $80.6%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $3$ dimensions would preserve $97.3%$ of the variance.

![](images/cc/ccc57a7e978a8b123dd21da151c2b0fec3080be9d39f1c8f26cc3b19c0cbd2b1.png)

Therefore, we should reduce the dataset to $3\text{ dimensions},$ since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance." :question/difficulty We should pick components based on $\text{the amount of cumulative variance preserved}.$

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

In our example, the singular values are

$$
{\sigma }_{1}=3.041,\,{\sigma }_{2}=1.967,\,{\sigma }_{3}=1.671,\,{\sigma }_{4}=0.268.
$$

Let us now compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first principal component is 

$$
\frac{{\sigma }_{1}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.041}^{2}}{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}+{1.671}^{2}+{0.268}^{2}}≈57.9%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{2}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}}{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}+{1.671}^{2}+{0.268}^{2}}≈82.1%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first three principal components is 

$$
\frac{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}{\sigma }_{i}^{2}}=\frac{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}+{1.671}^{2}}{{3.041}^{2}+{1.967}^{2}+{1.671}^{2}+{0.268}^{2}}≈99.6%.
$$

Thus, we obtain that

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $57.9%$ of the variance,

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $82.1%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $3$ dimensions would preserve $99.6%$ of the variance.

In order to reduce the dimensionality of the dataset, we will project the data onto the first few principal components, picking the number of components based on the amount of cumulative variance preserved.

The first step is to $\text{standardize the data}.$

The standardized data matrix is

$$
{X}_{\text{std}}=[\begin{aligned}0.98 & 1.40 & 1.50 \\ -0.08 & 0.70 & 0.20 \\ -1.32 & -0.79 & -1.12 \\ 0.99 & -0.45 & 0.09 \\ -0.57 & -0.85 & -0.67\end{aligned}].

$$
\begin{aligned}{X}_{\text{std}} & =UΣ{V}^{T},\,\text{where} \\ U & =[\begin{aligned}-0.701 & 0.221 & -0.466 & 0.493 & 0.003 \\ -0.148 & 0.419 & 0.689 & 0.249 & 0.516 \\ 0.579 & 0.314 & -0.029 & 0.657 & -0.367 \\ -0.107 & -0.812 & 0.296 & 0.492 & -0.005 \\ 0.375 & -0.137 & -0.469 & 0.146 & 0.774\end{aligned}], \\ Σ & =[\begin{aligned}3.215 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1.273 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.238 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}], \\ V & =[\begin{aligned}-0.547 & -0.751 & 0.370 \\ -0.564 & 0.657 & 0.500 \\ -0.619 & 0.065 & -0.783\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We compute the cumulative variance preserved for different numbers of components.

The variance along a principal component is equal to the corresponding eigenvalue of the covariance matrix, which is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value of the data matrix.

$$
\frac{{3.215}^{2}}{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}+{0.238}^{2}}≈86.0%.
$$

- The fraction of variance preserved by projecting the data onto the first two principal components is 

$$
\frac{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}}{{3.215}^{2}+{1.273}^{2}+{0.238}^{2}}≈99.5%.
$$

Thus, we have that 

- reducing the dataset to $1$ dimension would preserve $86.0%$ of the variance, while

- reducing the dataset to $2$ dimensions would preserve $99.5%$ of the variance.

If we wish to preserve $90%$ of the variance, we should reduce the dataset to $2\text{ dimensions}$ , since this is the minimum number of components that preserves at least $90%$ of the variance.

Writing ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}$ for the columns of $V$ and ${u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3},{u}_{4},{u}_{5}$ for the columns of $U$, the reduced dataset is

$$
{X}_{\text{red}}={X}_{\text{std}}\cdot [\begin{aligned}{v}_{1} & {v}_{2}\end{aligned}],
$$

since we need to project the data onto the first two principal components, which are the first two columns of $V.$

{u}_{2}\end{aligned}]}^{T}\cdot {X}_{\text{std}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205206 :tutorial/content "In previous lessons, we learned that the principal components of a standardized data matrix $X$ are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, and that these eigenvectors appear as the columns of $V$ in the singular value decomposition $X = U\Sigma V^T.$ We also learned that the variance along each principal component is proportional to the square of the corresponding singular value.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to use principal components to perform **feature extraction** — the process of projecting high-dimensional data onto a lower-dimensional subspace while preserving as much variance as possible.

To illustrate the idea, suppose a biologist has recorded the resting heart rate and breathing rate for four mammals of different sizes. Both measurements have been standardized, giving the $4 \times 2$ data matrix

![](images/c6/c6952e27be521fed69a3e9ff76520b01873fdc3e3e28f0015550cbdc8cda3110.svg)

The biologist knows that body size strongly influences both heart rate and breathing rate — smaller animals tend to have faster rates for both. They want to extract a single "metabolic index" that captures this underlying factor. How should they proceed?

From the SVD $X = U\Sigma V^T,$ the first principal component is

![](images/82/82a177ec2b7448d62d171a249e464d5da15308e41a6140b156d2d50d2c251f00.svg)

which points in the direction of maximum variance. To obtain a one-dimensional representation of the data, we project each row of $X$ onto this direction by computing

![](images/39/39fa24e5c2dbec4ceb7a56c0ee17f9c4996d08a2d9e1bc91d0849d7e24abe5c1.svg)

The result is a $4 \times 1$ vector — one number per animal — that captures the variation in body size. The second animal, with the most negative standardized values (indicating a larger, slower-metabolizing animal), has the largest projected value." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205213 :tutorial/content "More generally, suppose we have a standardized $n \times p$ data matrix $X,$ where each row is a data point and each column is a feature. To reduce the data from $p$ dimensions to $k$ dimensions, we project the data onto the first $k$ principal components. If $V_k$ is the $p \times k$ matrix whose columns are the first $k$ principal components, the reduced data matrix is

$$
Z = X V_k.
$$

Each row of $Z$ is a $k$-dimensional representation of the corresponding data point, expressed in terms of the principal component directions.

There is an equivalent way to compute $Z$ using the SVD. Starting from $X = U\Sigma V^T,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Z & =X{V}_{k} \\  & =UΣ{V}^{T}{V}_{k} \\  & =UΣ[\begin{aligned}{I}_{k} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =U[\begin{aligned}{Σ}_{k} \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={U}_{k}{Σ}_{k},\end{aligned}
$$

where $U_k$ is the $n \times k$ matrix of the first $k$ columns of $U,$ and $\Sigma_k$ is the $k \times k$ diagonal matrix of the first $k$ singular values. 

So, we can compute the reduced data either as $XV_k$ or as $U_k\Sigma_k.$

**Watch out!** The vector $v_1$ (the first column of $V$) is a *direction* — a unit vector in feature space pointing along maximum variance. By contrast, the product $Xv_1$ (equivalently, $u_1\sigma_1$) is the *projected data* — an $n \times 1$ vector giving each data point's coordinate along that direction. Some texts refer to this projected data as "the first principal component of the data" or as "scores," so the term "principal component" can mean either the direction or the projected values, depending on context." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205214 :tutorial/content "In the previous section, we saw how to project data onto the first $k$ principal components. But how do we choose $k?$ Keeping more components preserves more information, while keeping fewer gives a more compact representation at the cost of discarding some variation.

Recall that the variance along the $i$th principal component is proportional to $\sigma_i^2,$ where $\sigma_i$ is the $i$th singular value. Therefore, the fraction of total variance preserved by keeping the first $k$ components is

$$
\dfrac{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \cdots + \sigma_k^2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 + \cdots + \sigma_p^2} = \dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{p} \sigma_i^2}.
$$

While the amount of variance we need to preserve depends on the application, as a rule of thumb, we will choose the smallest $k$ that preserves at least $90\%$ of the variance. That is, we select $k$ such that

$$
\dfrac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k} \sigma_i^2}{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{p} \sigma_i^2} \geq 0.90.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186205215 :tutorial/content "We can now summarize the complete pipeline for using PCA to extract features from a dataset.

1\. **Standardize the data.** Subtract the mean of each feature and divide by its standard deviation. This ensures that all features contribute equally to the analysis, regardless of their original units or scales.

2\. **Compute the SVD.** Find the singular value decomposition $X_{\text{std}} = U\Sigma V^T.$ The columns of $V$ are the principal components, and the diagonal entries of $\Sigma$ are the singular values.

3\. **Choose the number of components.** Using the singular values, compute the cumulative variance for each possible choice of $k$ and select the smallest $k$ that preserves at least $90\%$ of the variance.

4\. **Project the data.** Compute the reduced data matrix $Z = X_{\text{std}} V_k,$ where $V_k$ consists of the first $k$ columns of $V.$

To interpret results in terms of the original features or to apply the same transformation to new data, we must keep track of the means and standard deviations used in Step 1." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186204154 :activity/expected-seconds 1440.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186112039 :answer-field/choices 17592186112040] [:db/retract 17592186112039 :answer-field/choices 17592186112041] [:db/retract 17592186112039 :answer-field/choices 17592186112042] [:db/retract 17592186112039 :answer-field/choices 17592186112043] [:db/retract 17592186112039 :answer-field/choices 17592186112044] {:db/id 17592186115271 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-cf71d35a-0b9f-5563-8501-c0ec218240c0" "question-cd81b926-79ef-579e-9c6d-82f75c5992d4"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115100 :question/problem "Simplify $\dfrac {x^2 - 9} {(x + 3)(x+2)}.$" :question/worked-solution "The numerator is a difference of squares. "q-14337" :question/problem "Which of the following is equivalent to $\frac{4{d}^{2}-36}{2(d+3)}?$" :question/worked-solution "The numerator is a difference of squares. It can be factored as

$$
4{d}^{2}-36=4({d}^{2}-9)=4(d+3)(d-3).
$$

Canceling out any common factors that appear in the numerator and the denominator, we get

For example, to simplify the rational expression $\dfrac{2x}{2+6x},$ we cancel out a factor of $2$ from the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x}{2+6x} & = \\ \frac{2x}{2(1+3x)} & = \\ \frac{x}{1+3x}\end{aligned}
$$

Sometimes, however, we can have more complicated expressions which require **polynomial factorization** in order to be simplified.

No need to panic though! The main strategy is always the same: factor the numerator and denominator, and then cancel out common factors.

For example, to simplify the rational expression $\dfrac{x^2-4}{x+2},$ we factor the difference of squares in the numerator and then cancel out a common factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}-4}{x+2} & = \\ \frac{(x+2)(x-2)}{x+2} & = \\ \frac{\cancel{(x+2)}(x-2)}{\cancel{x+2}} & = \\ x-2 & \end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115452 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186124629 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-f1d7f6a4-6114-5671-a52c-7df48bee5e24"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-f1d7f6a4-6114-5671-a52c-7df48bee5e24" :question/id #uuid "f1d7f6a4-6114-5671-a52c-7df48bee5e24" :question/math-academy-id "q-141342" :question/problem "Consider the following sentence:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ then  $\text{__________}\,.$*

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?

I. $\text{Null}(A)$ has no basis

II. $A$ is **not** invertible

III. All columns of $A$ are pivot columns" :question/worked-solution "The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=n=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately. 

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{Null}(A)$ has no basis.* $\,\times $ 

Since $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ we have $\text{Null}(A)\ne \{0\}$ which, in turn, means that $\text{Null}(A)$ must have a basis.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $A$ is **not** invertible.* $\,✓$

Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A)\ne 0,$ we must have that $A$ is **not** invertible.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.* $\,\times $

Since $A$ is not invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{n},$ which means that not all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-20580d7d-28aa-5c7c-a048-784d0bfa2d4b"] :db/ensure "question-74f4be02-4fe9-5741-a4d1-7268f77a2f5f" :question/id #uuid "74f4be02-4fe9-5741-a4d1-7268f77a2f5f" :question/math-academy-id "q-142472" :question/problem "Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix and  $det(A)=-1?$ 

I. $A$ is **not** invertible

II. $\text{rank}(A)=3$

III. $A$ has $4$ pivot columns" :question/worked-solution "Since $A$ is a $3\times 3$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=3=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. Indeed,   a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ Since here we have $det(A)=-1\ne 0,$ our matrix $A$ must be invertible.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem
$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\text{rank}(A)=3.$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{rank}(A)=3$,  it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))=3$ which, in turn, means that  $A$ has $3$ pivot columns, not $4.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-255a02e5-2e2c-5989-905e-69f5223274a6"] :db/ensure "![](images/f3/f33fde62793530cfe8970a9fea690fc71036312483ea617088a8d0a663d5133a.png)

Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$ for $-\frac{\pi }{6}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{6},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta ,
$$

where $r(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta )$, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\theta ))}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{cos}^{2}⁡(3\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =(\theta +\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\theta )){|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =(\frac{\pi }{6}-(-\frac{\pi }{6}))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\pi )) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}+0 \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-451b0468-1ab6-5622-abf5-d01927a565b8"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-451b0468-1ab6-5622-abf5-d01927a565b8" :answer-field/id #uuid "451b0468-1ab6-5622-abf5-d01927a565b8" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-f1ffe733-727d-5ca8-9de6-2f0a4144bd80" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f1ffe733-727d-5ca8-9de6-2f0a4144bd80"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f1ffe733-727d-5ca8-9de6-2f0a4144bd80" :answer/id #uuid "f1ffe733-727d-5ca8-9de6-2f0a4144bd80" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-86ea583e-6e3e-5bb4-93ab-14ccfe18681c" :question/id #uuid "86ea583e-6e3e-5bb4-93ab-14ccfe18681c" :question/math-academy-id "q-352297" :question/problem "Find the area $A$ bounded by the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}.$ Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{2}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=0$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{2}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(9{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+5{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +12\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(4+\frac{5(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))}{2}+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{13}{2}-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{13}{2}\theta -\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )){|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{13\pi }{4}+6) \\  & =3+\frac{13\pi }{8} \\  & =\frac{13\pi +24}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-2b1fe94c-bcca-5ef1-b698-9fc1476d4a23"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-2b1fe94c-bcca-5ef1-b698-9fc1476d4a23" :answer-field/id #uuid "2b1fe94c-bcca-5ef1-b698-9fc1476d4a23" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-622acefd-6fc4-5289-acf9-eacb640ce3ef" :answer-field/choices ["answer-622acefd-6fc4-5289-acf9-eacb640ce3ef"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-622acefd-6fc4-5289-acf9-eacb640ce3ef" :answer/id #uuid "622acefd-6fc4-5289-acf9-eacb640ce3ef" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "3+\frac{13\pi}{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186093357 :tutorial/content "Suppose we want to find the area of the region bounded by the polar curve $r = 3\cos\theta$ and the rays $\theta_1 = 0$ and $\theta_2 = \dfrac{\pi}{2},$ as shown in blue in the picture below. Can we calculate this area using polar coordinates?

![](images/2c/2c7e638a338aed2155ef5bf388be1f83a3a67d2296d5be09987b099a07edacbd.png)

In general, the area of the region bounded by a polar curve $r=r(\theta)$ and the rays $\theta=\theta_1$ and $\theta=\theta_2$ is given by the formula

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2 \:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Therefore, the area of the half-circle above can be obtained as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\theta {|}_{0}^{\pi /2}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta ){|}_{0}^{\pi /2}) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{\pi }{2}+0) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{8}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186093452 :tutorial/content "We've been using the following formula for the area of the region bounded by a polar curve ![](images/70/7031a0f3ab71df36bc36e925fcf4f04dbfc4feec5f374092855ef8d97b104452.svg) and the rays ![](images/38/38b971de9610efe2ed0de9f10956c73cf5cd967a86a5bcbb076791f369c22bef.svg) and ![](images/81/818e2605a585628c4becd20664b58007dbd2348ca664c80be6a838868a64693a.svg)

![](images/55/55ffcf934c3a9e33a3376fa1796e6fb68ad1198d719db5ea094fe8eb46c5f47d.svg)

But where does this formula come from?

To see where the formula comes from, we can think about breaking up the area bounded by a polar curve into infinitesimally small sectors of circles.

As shown in the graph below, each sector has a radius of ![](images/3a/3a4ef1c1b261a53f9c45d0c90f2d44b155125fe1e7b1359406830111b4846f2f.svg) and spans an infinitesimally small angle, ![](images/09/0904a69fa5e6a3a10eaf74b3fdd865db92761eeeffffae1c0badd33ffdf5b34b.svg)

![](images/82/82be86e7092a97ca5b2f1423f32b15030af0c8c63bf47ece8be40b45720ac905.png)

The ratio of the area of a sector to the full area of the circle must be the same as the ratio of the angle of the sector to a full revolution of the circle. {:db/id 17592186055952 :tutorial/content "Consider the graph of the parabola ![](images/f2/f218c572691a74963cd3808bf4df2923122e84b65d1fabf1138bab6264b043b5.svg) shown below.

![](images/45/450251899f728a3cc927b72fdb7655204828c8e0be0432cb08cee2462d6e5bfe.png)

We can describe many features of the graph using mathematical terminology:

- The ![](images/fc/fcc5df999e3b49fae1685ee0ab5bd03709804e1dd49f2ee722c4269eb0f5506d.svg)-intercepts of the parabola are at ![](images/81/8171bb8403bd612f56ef5f32f400f1aef8efeed51ea279d36779771fdea1ae0d.svg) and ![](images/77/779cec712506e0f798805963ab85841b46650fb22681d97a64aec4b85a47d07f.svg) We say that ![](images/b0/b064281df4bef2506521322c7477468b9cc565616e2c5b6f21000df6522399c1.svg) and ![](images/1f/1fb9f2f73a09599931892c1dee7629975b4d851e5dd6f0d07b7c641bbf17bf54.svg) are the **roots** (or **zeros**) of the parabola.

\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}, & {x}^{2}\le y\le 1,\,0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}(1-{x}^{2}), & 0<x<1 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the expression for the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ for $0<x<1.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{\frac{3}{2}(1-{x}^{2})} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}^{2}\le y\le 1,\,0<x<1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\cdot \,\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{{x}^{2}}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}[\frac{1}{2}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{1-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{1-{x}^{4}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{1-{x}^{2}}}\cdot \frac{\cancel{(1-{x}^{2})}(1+{x}^{2})}{2} \\  & =\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186159686 :answer-field/correct "answer-7cfb93cf-bd42-5bbd-b926-c729076a7176" :answer-field/choices ["answer-9d05d328-ed87-5676-8000-bf330c49b276" "answer-f86d5c54-dcc9-590b-831d-717992f4b407" "answer-fd4e3252-f147-5beb-9e9a-fc41e8f66725" "answer-7cfb93cf-bd42-5bbd-b926-c729076a7176" "answer-e1e11f88-ae8b-5b32-bcc7-944cd00e9429"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9d05d328-ed87-5676-8000-bf330c49b276" :answer/id #uuid "9d05d328-ed87-5676-8000-bf330c49b276" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1+x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f86d5c54-dcc9-590b-831d-717992f4b407" :answer/id #uuid "f86d5c54-dcc9-590b-831d-717992f4b407" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-x" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fd4e3252-f147-5beb-9e9a-fc41e8f66725" :answer/id #uuid "fd4e3252-f147-5beb-9e9a-fc41e8f66725" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1-{x}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7cfb93cf-bd42-5bbd-b926-c729076a7176" :answer/id #uuid "7cfb93cf-bd42-5bbd-b926-c729076a7176" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1+{x}^{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e1e11f88-ae8b-5b32-bcc7-944cd00e9429" :answer/id #uuid "e1e11f88-ae8b-5b32-bcc7-944cd00e9429" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162127 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-c0901d8a-5ab9-5481-aeea-fb9811603032" "question-febf3d13-3a80-5fb8-bb8d-fc4ac7755bf9" "question-72ca9ca6-7469-59a8-9b29-546c35450d5e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-c0901d8a-5ab9-5481-aeea-fb9811603032" :question/id #uuid "c0901d8a-5ab9-5481-aeea-fb9811603032" :question/math-academy-id "q-146256" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3(x+y)}{4}, & 0<x\le 2y,\,\,0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}3{y}^{2}, & 0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3(x+y)}{4})}{3{y}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(x+y)}{4{y}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0<x\le 2y,\,0<y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{(x+1)}{4}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{(x+1)}{4}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}({x}^{2}+x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(\frac{8}{3}+2)-0] \\  & =\frac{7}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e0a449ce-c8fa-55c9-ab8d-6d9f7f6b2000"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e0a449ce-c8fa-55c9-ab8d-6d9f7f6b2000" :answer-field/id #uuid "e0a449ce-c8fa-55c9-ab8d-6d9f7f6b2000" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-d7d6410d-8ce9-57d1-9928-c24c78a23343" :answer-field/choices ["answer-92fa2249-5af2-5ed4-b4f5-e80a0891b31b" "answer-c7e58acf-da9e-5137-9d01-db3f88e60768" "answer-a59e2126-217b-588b-8ec1-c18e748c0160" "answer-02c49c4a-231f-5e98-b371-0e935a20a3ea" "answer-d7d6410d-8ce9-57d1-9928-c24c78a23343"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-92fa2249-5af2-5ed4-b4f5-e80a0891b31b" :answer/id #uuid "92fa2249-5af2-5ed4-b4f5-e80a0891b31b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c7e58acf-da9e-5137-9d01-db3f88e60768" :answer/id #uuid "c7e58acf-da9e-5137-9d01-db3f88e60768" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a59e2126-217b-588b-8ec1-c18e748c0160" :answer/id #uuid "a59e2126-217b-588b-8ec1-c18e748c0160" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{4}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-02c49c4a-231f-5e98-b371-0e935a20a3ea" :answer/id #uuid "02c49c4a-231f-5e98-b371-0e935a20a3ea" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d7d6410d-8ce9-57d1-9928-c24c78a23343" :answer/id #uuid "d7d6410d-8ce9-57d1-9928-c24c78a23343" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-febf3d13-3a80-5fb8-bb8d-fc4ac7755bf9" :question/id #uuid "febf3d13-3a80-5fb8-bb8d-fc4ac7755bf9" :question/math-academy-id "q-146344" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}1+y-x, & 0\le x\le 2y,\,\,0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}2y, & 0<y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $Y$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1].$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $X$ given $Y=y$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=y]$ is a function of $y.$ 

The conditional density function of $X$ given $Y=y$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{Y}(y)} \\  & =\frac{(1+y-x)}{2y},\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le x\le 2y,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=0.$ 

Now, substituting $y=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y),$ we get

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)=\frac{(2-x)}{2}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X\,|\,Y=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }x\,{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,1)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\cdot \frac{(2-x)}{2}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(4-\frac{8}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b1e89487-9f71-5b83-9a7d-94bccae434fa"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b1e89487-9f71-5b83-9a7d-94bccae434fa" :answer-field/id #uuid "b1e89487-9f71-5b83-9a7d-94bccae434fa" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-76810779-d00b-5526-95a9-f6b537df2534" :answer-field/choices ["answer-05ef324f-e3e0-55de-bf8c-31d0adf63779" "answer-76810779-d00b-5526-95a9-f6b537df2534" "answer-1433506f-2bda-51e6-9d54-5354fc116b88" "answer-1d68d2b6-b709-52d4-a640-81aa11b499e7" "answer-ac4f0db2-b37d-5e05-b26f-af89dbb0df5e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-05ef324f-e3e0-55de-bf8c-31d0adf63779" :answer/id #uuid "05ef324f-e3e0-55de-bf8c-31d0adf63779" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76810779-d00b-5526-95a9-f6b537df2534" :answer/id #uuid "76810779-d00b-5526-95a9-f6b537df2534" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1433506f-2bda-51e6-9d54-5354fc116b88" :answer/id #uuid "1433506f-2bda-51e6-9d54-5354fc116b88" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3}{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1d68d2b6-b709-52d4-a640-81aa11b499e7" :answer/id #uuid "1d68d2b6-b709-52d4-a640-81aa11b499e7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5}{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ac4f0db2-b37d-5e05-b26f-af89dbb0df5e" :answer/id #uuid "ac4f0db2-b37d-5e05-b26f-af89dbb0df5e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{8}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-72ca9ca6-7469-59a8-9b29-546c35450d5e" :question/id #uuid "72ca9ca6-7469-59a8-9b29-546c35450d5e" :question/math-academy-id "q-146353" :question/problem "$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2+y-x}{3}, & 0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\,{f}_{X}(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5-2x}{6}, & 0\le x\le 1, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $X$ and $Y$  be continuous random variables. Their joint probability density function and the marginal probability density function of $X$ are shown above. Find the conditional expected value $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1].$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the conditional expected value of $Y$ given $X=x$ is defined by

$$
\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)\,\text{d}y.
$$

Note that $\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=x]$ is a function of $x.$ 

The conditional density function of $Y$ given $X=x$ can be computed as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x) & =\frac{f(x,y)}{{f}_{X}(x)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2+y-x}{3})}{(\frac{5-2x}{6})} \\  & =\frac{2(2+y-x)}{5-2x},\end{aligned}
$$

 

where $0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 1.$ Outside this domain, we have ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=0.$

Now, substituting $x=1$ into the expression for ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x),$ we get

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)=\frac{2(2+y-1)}{5-2\cdot 1}=\frac{2(1+y)}{3}.
$$

Therefore, using the definition of the conditional expectation above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[Y\,|\,X=1] & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }y\,{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y\cdot \frac{2(1+y)}{3}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y+{y}^{2})\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3})-0] \\  & =\frac{5}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-52b89aa0-9d44-5e08-ab59-3cc05bb04a17"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id and $\dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n}} = -0.4$ for all integers $n \geq 1,$ find the value of $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_{n}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the given series is a geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <    1,
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
a_1=-2.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_{n}} = -0.4.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-2}{1-(-0.4)} \\  & =\frac{-2}{1.4} \\  & =-\frac{10}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092254 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-fbd76d75-8ee7-5bcd-acb2-1f5ae9aa3787" "question-df45f3a3-f545-5c42-98d5-edf671e88e36" "question-5c0c2f91-9457-576f-ab5b-77c8f4a530ad" "question-56e0e8e1-0cfd-5d25-b2ed-327a18d60529" "question-7e8589d7-77a6-5ea2-bd7d-7f7a24b35382"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092106 :question/problem "Evaluate the series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty 2(0.5)^{n}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$ 

The sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <    1,
$$

where $a_1$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is 

$$
a_1 = 2(0.5)^{1} = 1.
$$

 

The common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{2(0.5)^2}{2(0.5)^1} = 0.5.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }2(0.5)^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{1}{1-0.5} \\  & =\frac{1}{0.5} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092182 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-dd479934-e321-5035-bf71-51bd7984a9a8" "question-54f15411-79a5-546c-8ee4-965cb1e88cd5" "question-d588b5a8-8a0c-5e4d-8e17-d8c93ee42445" "question-75a391e4-92f0-5306-8519-d804235fa403"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092019 :question/problem "Evaluate the series $\displaystyle \sum_{n=2}^\infty\left(\dfrac 2 3\right)^n.$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that the index $n$ starts from $2.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$ 

In this case, the first term is $a_2,$ and so the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_2}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <        1.
$$

For the first few terms, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2} & ={(\frac{2}{3})}^{2}=\frac{4}{9} \\ {a}_{3} & ={(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}=\frac{8}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

The common ratio is:

$$
r = \dfrac{a_3}{a_2} = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{8}{27}\right)}{\left( \dfrac{4}{9}\right)} = \dfrac 2 3
$$

So, the sum of the series is:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=2}^{\infty }{(\frac{2}{3})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{2}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{9})}{(1-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4}{9})}{(\frac{1}{3})} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 3}{9} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092256 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-4db8cfdc-3e22-5283-b109-341d9daf5b09" "question-7a6fcb51-44e7-59f8-9078-8afece3073a1" "question-499dc119-15d3-5a33-9631-8bc1b2a65d1c"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092108 :question/problem "Evaluate the geometric series $\displaystyle \sum_{n=3}^\infty \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2n}.$" :question/worked-solution "First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3.$ In this case, the first term is $a_3,$ and so the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of this geometric series is given by

$$
S_\infty = \dfrac{a_3}{1-r}, \qquad |r| <        1.
$$

Computing the first few terms, we get:

$$
a_3 = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2(3)} = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{6} = 5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{7}
$$

 

$$
a_4 = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2(4)} = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{8} = 5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{9}
$$

Therefore, the common ratio is

$$
r = \dfrac{a_4}{a_3} = \dfrac{5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{9}}{5\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{7}} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{1}{4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=3}^{\infty }\frac{5}{2}{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2n} & =\frac{{a}_{3}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{5{(\frac{1}{2})}^{7}}{(1-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{5}{128})}{(\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =(\frac{5}{128})(\frac{4}{3}) \\  & =\frac{5}{3(32)} \\  & =\frac{5}{96}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-14f76056-5e3c-539d-8f82-855878eb07d3" :question/id #uuid "14f76056-5e3c-539d-8f82-855878eb07d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-50498" :question/problem "Given that ${a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}$ and $\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}$ for all integers $n\ge 1,$ find the value of ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n}.$" :question/worked-solution "Notice that the given series is geometric series because the ratio of any two consecutive terms is constant.

The sum to infinity ${S}_{\infty }$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

$$
{S}_{\infty }=\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r},\,|r|<1,
$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$
{a}_{1}=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}=-\frac{1}{10}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(1-(-\frac{1}{10}))} \\  & =\frac{-\frac{5}{2}}{(\frac{11}{10})} \\  & =-\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{10}{11} \\  & =-\frac{25}{11}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4409dd34-9ab8-5a98-a1d2-9602397921b0"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

$$

where ${a}_{1}$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

We're told that the first term is

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }{a}_{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{5}{(1-(-0.2))} \\  & =\frac{5}{(1+0.2)} \\  & =\frac{5}{1.2} \\  & =\frac{25}{6}.\end{aligned}

$$

The sum $S_\infty$ of an infinite geometric series is given by the formula

$$
S_{\infty} = \dfrac {\color{black}a_1} {1 - {\color{black}r}},
$$

where ${\color{black}r}$ is the common ratio and $\color{black}a_1$ is the first term. So, we need to determine $\color{black}a_1$ and $\color{black}r$ and then plug those values into this formula.

The first term is

$$
{\color{black}a_1} = 3 \left( \dfrac 1 4 \right)^1 = {\color{black}\dfrac 3 4},
$$

and the common ratio is 

$$
{\color{black}r} = \dfrac {a_2}{\color{black}a_1} = \dfrac {3 \left (\dfrac 1 4 \right)^2}{3\left( \dfrac 1 4 \right)^1}= {\color{black}\dfrac 1 4}.
$$

So, the sum of the series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }3{(\frac{1}{4})}^{n} & =\frac{{a}_{1}}{1-r} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{4})}{(1-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{4})}{(\frac{3}{4})} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092404 :activity/expected-seconds 840.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186134402 :question/answer-fields 17592186132451] {:db/id 17592186133814 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6e2c74ef-5be6-50fe-9eda-c944716ab881" "question-01f92ee9-73cd-5c08-adfa-addc2317087e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133629 :question/problem "An inner product on $V = \mathbb{R}^3$ is defined as $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle =  2x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2 + 3x_3 y_3.$

Calculate the norm of the vector $v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ under this inner product." :question/worked-solution "The norm of a vector $v$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $‖v‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
⟨x(t),y(t)⟩=x(0)y(0)+x(1)y(1)+x(2)y(2).
$$

Calculate the norm of the vector $p(t)=3t-2{t}^{2}.$" :question/worked-solution "The norm of a vector $p(t)$ with respect to an inner product $⟨\cdot ,\cdot ⟩$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖=\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $p(t)=3t-2{t}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
p(0)=0,\,p(1)=1,\,p(2)=-2.
$$

Computing $‖p(t)‖$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖p(t)‖ & =\sqrt{⟨p(t),p(t)⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{p(0)p(0)+p(1)p(1)+p(2)p(2)} \\  & =\sqrt{[p(0)]^{2}+[p(1)]^{2}+[p(2)]^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(0)^{2}+(1)^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+1+4} \\  & =\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-4a799a47-68c0-5f48-82fe-456dcddb2abb"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-4a799a47-68c0-5f48-82fe-456dcddb2abb" :answer-field/id #uuid "4a799a47-68c0-5f48-82fe-456dcddb2abb" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-1fa00b09-aa2e-5df4-ac96-221f4752071a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-3425195d-9aff-555f-aedc-3c2ff2394fd5" "answer-5a6813eb-8d5c-5891-9a6f-a20bbd0d60b9" "answer-a269ca2f-0828-50e2-9c13-2e3788349d15" "answer-1fa00b09-aa2e-5df4-ac96-221f4752071a" "answer-116df7c4-ec26-5aa2-9b40-416a961b75bd"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3425195d-9aff-555f-aedc-3c2ff2394fd5" :answer/id #uuid "3425195d-9aff-555f-aedc-3c2ff2394fd5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5a6813eb-8d5c-5891-9a6f-a20bbd0d60b9" :answer/id #uuid "5a6813eb-8d5c-5891-9a6f-a20bbd0d60b9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a269ca2f-0828-50e2-9c13-2e3788349d15" :answer/id #uuid "a269ca2f-0828-50e2-9c13-2e3788349d15" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{197}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1fa00b09-aa2e-5df4-ac96-221f4752071a" :answer/id #uuid "1fa00b09-aa2e-5df4-ac96-221f4752071a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{5}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-116df7c4-ec26-5aa2-9b40-416a961b75bd" :answer/id #uuid "116df7c4-ec26-5aa2-9b40-416a961b75bd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{7}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135035 :tutorial/content "Any vector space $V$ combined with an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ on $V$ is called an **inner product space.** 

When referring to inner product spaces, we often say that the vector space $V$ is *equipped* with the inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle.$

The **norm** of a vector $\mathbf v\in V$ in an inner product space is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

This definition allows us to apply the geometric concept of length to vectors defined in abstract vector spaces. This is because the norm of a vector $\mathbf v$ in an inner product space is a generalization of the norm (or length) of a vector in Euclidean space. To see this, recall that for $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^n,$ we have 

$$
\Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert = \sqrt{\mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{x}},
$$

and we have already seen that the dot product is itself an inner product.

Let's consider an example. Suppose that an inner product on $V = \mathbb{R}^3$ defined as 

$$
\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle =  3x_1 y_1 + 2x_2 y_2 + 2x_3 y_3.
$$

Now consider the vector $\mathbf v\in V,$ given by
![](images/46/46f92b1fb6f84950c98449deaab0c2574c10dfe01abe8c0c0d9258a57eee29ad.svg)

Computing $\|\mathbf{v}\|$ using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩} \\  & =\sqrt{3\cdot (1\cdot 1)+2\cdot (2\cdot 2)+2\cdot (1\cdot 1)} \\  & =\sqrt{3+8+2} \\  & =\sqrt{13}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186135036 :tutorial/content "Recall that a unit vector is a vector whose length is equal to $1.$ If we divide a non-zero vector $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb R^n$ by its norm $\Vert \mathbf{x} \Vert,$ we obtain a unit vector:

$$
\mathbf{u}=\dfrac{\mathbf{x}}{\Vert\mathbf{x}\Vert}
$$

The process of constructing a unit vector by dividing $\mathbf x$ by its norm is called **normalization.** 

We normalize vectors in more general inner product spaces using the same method. 

For example, consider an inner product on $V = \mathbb{R}^3$ defined as $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle =  2x_1 y_1 + 3x_2 y_2 + x_3 y_3.$  Let's normalize the following vector with respect to our inner product:  

![](images/40/40bcf2af70449b87fe001d3864642c88437aecca18bc0750cff09643dc2edc00.svg) 

The norm of a vector $\mathbf v$ with respect to an inner product $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle$ is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖=\sqrt{⟨v,v⟩}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the inner product using our definition, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨v,v⟩ & =2\cdot (2\cdot 2)+3\cdot (1\cdot 1)+2\cdot 2 \\  & =8+3+4 \\  & =15.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖v‖ & =\sqrt{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

To normalize the vector $\mathbf v$, we divide $\mathbf v$ by its norm $\|\mathbf v\| \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{v}{‖v‖} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{15}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{15}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186133985 :activity/expected-seconds 720.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100848 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-856534cf-3669-5864-adb1-aa4947ae5494"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100669 :question/problem "The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown below and the point $(0,9)$ lies on the curve. Sketch the graph of $y=f(x)-2.$

![](images/b0/b0c3acc57c74ced95e7387e285d9de1c629e7724fe9e111b13df209198069e8d.png)" :question/worked-solution "The graph of $y = f(x)$ passes through the point $(0, 9)$ as shown in the diagram.

So, the graph $y = f(x)$ would be $2$ units *below* the graph of $y = f(x) + 2.$

![](images/0c/0ce67d91fd6c15d97e882c785392f001a4f38ed9bedd50d8631b34e4d5543adc.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100849 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-3149eba2-f75e-505c-909c-9beed59b368d" "question-2b584399-1501-573d-8e9c-16d0bbc631a2"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100670 :question/problem "The point $A$ with coordinates $(2,-1)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x)$ and the point $B$ with coordinates $(2,-4)$ lies on the curve $y = g(x).$ If the curve $y = g(x)$ is related to $y = f(x)$ via the transformation $g(x) = f(x) + k$, then what is the value of $k?$" :question/worked-solution "First, notice that the point $B(2, -4)$ lies $3$ units *below* the point $A(2, -1).$ So, the graph of $y = g(x)$ can be obtained from the graph of $y = f(x)$ by shifting it $3$ units *down*. 

![](images/46/4656ae5ff75132fc9b760b6a8f73b0b434a8f66ecd621fa974a265df1d0d8a2c.png)

As a result, $k = -3.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100847 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b9eb1708-044c-5408-bdf8-03d4b09b76eb" "question-e09e1da8-e383-596f-bdbd-80147bb9fb19"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186100668 :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

The graph of $y = f(x)+3$ is obtained by translating the graph of $y=f(x)$ by $3$ units *up*. 

Hence, if the point $(3,4)$ lies on $y=f(x)$, then the point 

$$
(3,4+3) = (3,7)
$$

lies on $y=f(x) + 3.$

![](images/57/577911187229d6a56a8885e4cea2e25752615ed7bb807768abf4b54c5073d177.png)

**Method 2**

As $(3,4)$ lies on $y = f(x)$, we have that $f(3) = 4.$

Now, if $x = 3$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =f(3)+3 \\  & =4+3 \\  & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $(3,7)$ must lie on $y = f(x) + 3.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101206 :question/problem "![](images/82/82012efd1fbf78238ce1b6ecc49819283976db8f39ac5f57ec232a5eda8029dc.png)

"b9eb1708-044c-5408-bdf8-03d4b09b76eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-27000" :question/problem "The point $P$ with coordinates $(-3,1)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x)+1.$ Which of the following points must lie on $y=f(x)?$" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is obtained by translating the graph of $y=f(x)+1$ by $1$ unit *down.* 

Hence, if the point $(-3,1)$ lies on $y=f(x)+1$, then the point 

$$
(-3,1-1)=(-3,0)
$$

lies on $y=f(x).$

![](images/2c/2c76b54e0dc12d52fbc6e41a601d5e87a105537e055a9d4cee4c758b0dd3ae63.png)

**Method 2**

As $(-3,1)$ lies on $y=f(x)+1$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-3)+1 & =1 \\ f(-3) & =1-1 \\ f(-3) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $x=-3$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =f(-3) \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $(-3,0)$ must lie on $y=f(x).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-eda83d9c-61f5-554b-a3a6-fe587fe8ef1f"] :db/ensure "The point $P$ with coordinates $(-2,3)$ lies on the curve $y=f(x)+4.$ Which of the following points must lie on $y=f(x)?$" :question/worked-solution "**Method 1**

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is obtained by translating the graph of $y=f(x)+4$ by $4$ units *down.* 

Hence, if the point $(-2,3)$ lies on $y=f(x)+4$, then the point 

$$
(-2,3-4)=(-2,-1)
$$

lies on $y=f(x).$

![](images/5f/5f74a8d57dc1766912c4490ab156d0f7f2ed0bbc9b4dbb9e53ae46c48ceb8bb5.png)

**Method 2**

As $(-2,3)$ lies on $y=f(x)+4$, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-2)+4 & =3 \\ f(-2) & =3-4 \\ f(-2) & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, if $x=-2$ then

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =f(-2) \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the point $(-2,-1)$ must lie on $y=f(x).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-d83fabbc-abe9-5f4d-98e0-63937e6bc2ee"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-d83fabbc-abe9-5f4d-98e0-63937e6bc2ee" :answer-field/id #uuid "d83fabbc-abe9-5f4d-98e0-63937e6bc2ee" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-5c9182da-26b4-50dd-b999-b06ea4f26402" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5c9182da-26b4-50dd-b999-b06ea4f26402" "answer-7c0a67dc-b1bb-53f1-a28d-e4de8f2a5cf6" "answer-218a5463-3916-500e-8478-33f18275f486" "answer-1846fb2f-d11a-5c6c-8a8b-c56637894b4c" "answer-4b9120fe-c1c3-53ef-a361-99b8cca626c8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5c9182da-26b4-50dd-b999-b06ea4f26402" :answer/id #uuid "5c9182da-26b4-50dd-b999-b06ea4f26402" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-2,-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-7c0a67dc-b1bb-53f1-a28d-e4de8f2a5cf6" :answer/id #uuid "7c0a67dc-b1bb-53f1-a28d-e4de8f2a5cf6" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-2,0)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-218a5463-3916-500e-8478-33f18275f486" :answer/id #uuid "218a5463-3916-500e-8478-33f18275f486" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-2,1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1846fb2f-d11a-5c6c-8a8b-c56637894b4c" :answer/id #uuid "1846fb2f-d11a-5c6c-8a8b-c56637894b4c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-2,5)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4b9120fe-c1c3-53ef-a361-99b8cca626c8" :answer/id #uuid "4b9120fe-c1c3-53ef-a361-99b8cca626c8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-2,7)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101945 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we have the graph of $y=f(x)$ shown below. What would the graph of $y=f(x)+2$ look like, and how does it relate to the original curve?

![](images/1a/1a55ebd7e9dc656f3a2488debf14e63e655ed7548b76f63c26498f09d96d65ca.png)

For each point on the graph of $y=f(x)$ there is a corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x)+2$ with the same $x$-value and a $y$-value that is two units greater. So let's create a table of points.

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]} & \text{Points on [math]y=f(x)+2[/math]} \\ (-2,0) & (-2,2) \\ (0,1.5) & (0,3.5) \\ (1,2) & (1,4) \\ (3,-3) & (3,-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Every point on the graph of $y=f(x)+2$ is precisely two units above a point on the graph of $y=f(x)$. The graph of $y=f(x)+2$ is an **upward vertical translation** of the graph of $y=f(x)$ by two units.

![](images/66/6636d65acf9cd34d818d3d9e12a7b7de36dec4ceb70c7503a08751f971868855.png)

On the other hand, for each point on the graph of $y=f(x)$ there is a corresponding point on the graph of $y=f(x)-2$ with the same $x$-value and a $y$-value that is two units smaller. So let's create a table of points.

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]} & \text{Points on [math]y=f(x)-2[/math]} \\ (-2,0) & (-2,-2) \\ (0,1.5) & (0,-0.5) \\ (1,2) & (1,0) \\ (3,-3) & (3,-5)\end{aligned}
$$

Every point on the graph of $y=f(x)-2$ is two units below a point on the graph of $y=f(x)$. The graph of $y=f(x)-2$ is a **downward vertical translation** of the graph of $y=f(x)$ by two units.

![](images/72/72588aaa92f5b4bf9923c381cf5ad28ebb7288e77f6442549d0ffe1fdac3dc48.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101972 :tutorial/content "Consider the solid curve $y=f(x)$ and the dashed curve $y=f(x)+b$ shown below. What is the value of $b?$

![](images/b0/b058da1ea31e45f3029f1542642d802a35da7280f315a37ea92044e5c322fbd4.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)+b$ can be obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by translating it $6$ units down. So, $b=-6.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186101091 :activity/expected-seconds 420.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068913 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-ead518c9-914d-5e94-b01b-fb4224373ff4" "question-ecfb5c66-7387-5472-a64e-2ed6bd44ab74"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068525 :question/worked-solution "Remember that in general, the graph of $y=x^2+k$ looks like the standard parabola $y=x^2$ but translated $k$ units up. The vertex of $y=x^2+k$ is located at $(0,k).$

Here, the curve shown is the parabola $y=x^2$ after being translated $3$ units upward. The vertex is located at $(0,3).$

First, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for $x\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ \sqrt{x} & ={x}^{3} \\ x & ={x}^{6} \\ {x}^{6}-x & =0 \\ x({x}^{5}-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing *away* from the axis of rotation.

![](images/2a/2abe3a274ab5afee2bc0a85c48c2f1218620b86354c3c4e6e4dd8758ca1af5e5.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner function $y=g(x)=x^3,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $y=f(x)=\sqrt{x}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}([\text{outer}]^{2}-[\text{inner}]^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({[\sqrt{x}]}^{2}-{[{x}^{3}]}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}(x-{x}^{6})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068775 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a5df2e25-639b-5613-82c1-85dbfc89566d" "question-17abd4d5-764f-50c1-82c3-4fcec4b8a574" "question-61a0b761-b748-5011-958d-51f405f814ac"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186068617 :question/problem "![](images/73/7373418f2a0bac416e37662cea5a79101220820aa6f23c50a80fbf6addc5eefd.png)

\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}({[\text{outer}]}^{2}-{[\text{inner}]}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({[{x}^{2}]}^{2}-{[{x}^{5}]}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}-{x}^{10})\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {(\frac{{x}^{5}}{5}-\frac{{x}^{11}}{11})|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\pi [(\frac{1}{5}-\frac{1}{11})-0] \\  & =\frac{6\pi }{55}.\end{aligned}

$$

Now, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(y) & =g(y) \\ \sqrt[3]{y} & =y \\ y & ={y}^{3} \\ {y}^{3}-y & =0 \\ y({y}^{2}-1) & =0\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ 1-{x}^{2} & ={x}^{2}-2x+1 \\ 2{x}^{2}-2x & =0 \\ x(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the limits of integration are from $x=0$ to $x=1.$

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing *away* from the axis of rotation.

- *enters* the region through the inner function $y=g(x)={x}^{2}-2x+1,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $y=f(x)=1-{x}^{2}.$

$$

Consider the finite region above bounded by $y=2x+2$ and $y=\sqrt{4x+4},$ as shown above. Calculate the volume of the solid generated when this region is rotated $2\pi $ radians about the $x\text{-axis.}$" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=2x+2$ and $g(x)=\sqrt{4x+4}.$

First, we determine the limits of integration. To do that, we find the intersections of the curves by solving the following equation for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =g(x) \\ 2x+2 & =\sqrt{4x+4} \\ 2(x+1) & =\sqrt{4x+4} \\ 4(x+1)^{2} & =4x+4 \\ {x}^{2}+2x+1 & =x+1 \\ {x}^{2}+x & =0 \\ x(x+1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the limits of integration are from $x=-1$ to $x=0.$

Let's draw our vertical arrow through the region to determine the inner function and the outer function. The arrow should be pointing *away* from the axis of rotation.

![](images/0a/0a6bdcc071500ac8dd40143c3219a14c80fc73d543d7307cb2c880a22db793a3.png)

The vertical arrow 

- *enters* the region through the inner function $y=f(x)=2x+2,$ and

- *leaves* through the outer function $y=g(x)=\sqrt{4x+4}.$

Therefore, the integral that gives our volume is

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\pi {\int }_{a}^{b}([\text{outer}]^{2}-[\text{inner}]^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}({[\sqrt{4x+4}]}^{2}-{[2x+2]}^{2})\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}[4x+4-(2(x+1))^{2}]\text{d}x \\  & =\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}[4(x+1)-4({x}^{2}+2x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}[x+1-({x}^{2}+2x+1)]\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {\int }_{-1}^{0}(-{x}^{2}-x)\text{d}x \\  & =4\pi {(-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =4\pi (0-(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2})) \\  & =4\pi (\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-9c25b804-adcd-5109-97e9-a671522d2fa7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-9c25b804-adcd-5109-97e9-a671522d2fa7" :answer-field/id #uuid "9c25b804-adcd-5109-97e9-a671522d2fa7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c448d435-9bcd-595a-9b15-481488adc3cd" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c448d435-9bcd-595a-9b15-481488adc3cd" "answer-f7aa2104-1ab4-5d6d-8862-d71d4c61233f" "answer-99d1f1a0-32aa-5964-8ea7-584cb8f97f59" "answer-48706475-0664-565e-bd2d-7f83441bc4d8" "answer-c948edf4-7c1a-595a-9006-e62d1d1f4937"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c448d435-9bcd-595a-9b15-481488adc3cd" :answer/id #uuid "c448d435-9bcd-595a-9b15-481488adc3cd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f7aa2104-1ab4-5d6d-8862-d71d4c61233f" :answer/id #uuid "f7aa2104-1ab4-5d6d-8862-d71d4c61233f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{5\pi }{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-99d1f1a0-32aa-5964-8ea7-584cb8f97f59" :answer/id #uuid "99d1f1a0-32aa-5964-8ea7-584cb8f97f59" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-48706475-0664-565e-bd2d-7f83441bc4d8" :answer/id #uuid "48706475-0664-565e-bd2d-7f83441bc4d8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c948edf4-7c1a-595a-9006-e62d1d1f4937" :answer/id #uuid "c948edf4-7c1a-595a-9006-e62d1d1f4937" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{6}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186069261 :question/problem "![](images/3f/3f27cf1fddfbbbdb9dd2593567743494ae15e061bca8d1e111ac1f1561561943.png)
